Tallowmarket is a B2B marketplace where independent restaurants buy directly from regional farms and ranches. - 5+ years of professional backend experience in Go, Java or Kotlin.
- Deep PostgreSQL knowledge: indexing, locking, isolation levels, and safe online migrations.
- Experience with event-driven systems (Kafka, Kinesis or similar) and idempotent processing.
- A track record of leading multi-engineer projects from design doc to launch.
- Clear written communication; we make most decisions in design docs.

NICE TO HAVE
- Prior work on a double-entry ledger or a payments platform.

Base salary band: $172,000 - $208,000 USD, plus equity and a 6% 401(k) match. This role is leveled at L5 (Senior).

Recruiter screen (30 minutes), a 60-minute ledger design exercise, a Go coding session, and a values conversation with our Director of Engineering, Imani Castellanos.

HTECH-CTX-G1.title: Tallowmarket Go coding session pre-read: Escrow Hold Overlap
HTECH-CTX-G1.text:
TALLOWMARKET - GO CODING SESSION PRE-READ
Problem: Escrow Hold Overlap (version 2)

Background
When a restaurant places an order, Tallowmarket places an escrow hold on the funds until the grower confirms delivery. Our Risk team wants to know how many holds are open at the same time, because the banking partner charges a fee tier based on the peak number of simultaneous holds in a day.

Part A (required)
You are given n holds. Each hold has an id, a start minute and an end minute. A hold covers the half-open interval [start, end): it is active at minute start and no longer active at minute end. Two holds that touch (one ends at 40, the other starts at 40) do not overlap.
Return two integers: the maximum number of holds active at the same instant, and the earliest instant at which that maximum is reached. If n is 0, return "0 -1".

Constraints
- 0 <= n <= 200,000
- 0 <= start < end <= 1,000,000,000 (integers, minutes since the start of the settlement epoch)
- Holds are NOT sorted. Ids are unique strings of up to 12 characters.
- Target: O(n log n) time. Your solution runs with a 2 second limit and 256 MB of memory.

Example 1
Input:
H1 10 50
H2 20 40
H3 40 70
H4 45 60
H5 70 90
Output: 3 45
Explanation: at minute 45, H1, H3 and H4 are active. At minute 40, H2 has already ended, so only H1 and H3 are active there.

Example 2
Input:
H1 5 15
H2 15 25
H3 25 35
Output: 1 5

Example 3
Input: (no holds)
Output: 0 -1

Part B (required)
Each hold also carries amount_cents, a positive integer up to 50,000,000. Return the maximum total amount_cents held at the same instant and the earliest instant it is reached. Use a 64-bit integer; the sum can exceed 2^31.

Example 4
Input:
H1 0 30 5000
H2 10 20 9000
H3 20 40 7000
Output: 14000 10
Explanation: during [10, 20) H1 and H2 are both held, 14000 in total. At minute 20, H2 ends and H3 starts, so the total drops to H1 + H3 = 12000.

Part C (discussion only, no code)
Holds will eventually arrive as a stream from Kafka, up to 50,000 inserts per second at peak, and a hold may also be cancelled before its end minute. Describe how you would keep the Part A answer current after each insert or cancel. We care about the data structure and its complexity, not a full implementation.

What we look at
- Correct handling of touching intervals. This is the most common mistake we see.
- Tie-breaking: when the maximum is reached more than once, report the earliest instant.
- Clear naming and small functions. Standard library only; no third-party packages.
- A few table-driven tests.

Please do not share this problem publicly. Questions about the statement can be raised with the session interviewer at the start of the call.

HTECH-CTX-G2.title: Dockhand design summary v1.3 (candidate project)
HTECH-CTX-G2.text:
DOCKHAND - Design Summary (v1.3)
Author: Tobias Venkataraman | Larkspur Freight, Platform Backend | Last updated: 2024-11-18
Status: in production since June 2024

1. Purpose
Dockhand moves shipment status events (picked up, in transit, delayed, delivered, exception) from the services that record them into Kafka, so that billing, the customer portal and the carrier-settlement services from Project Tern can react without polling the database. Volume is about 2.3 million events per day on average, with a morning peak of roughly 410 events per second between 07:30 and 09:00 Eastern.

2. Why an outbox
Before Dockhand, services wrote to PostgreSQL and then published to Kafka in the same request. When the publish failed after the commit, the event was lost; when the commit failed after the publish, consumers saw an event for a change that never happened. Dockhand uses a transactional outbox: the service writes the business row and an outbox row in the same PostgreSQL transaction. Nothing is published inside the request.

3. Components
- outbox_events table: one row per event (event_id UUID, shipment_id, event_type, payload JSONB, created_at, published_at). Partitioned by day; partitions older than 72 hours are dropped by a scheduled job, which is cheaper than DELETE plus vacuum.
- Relay: a Go service that polls unpublished rows every 250 ms in batches of up to 500, ordered by created_at, publishes them, then sets published_at. Two relay instances run, but only one is active at a time: the active one holds a PostgreSQL advisory lock. If it dies, the standby acquires the lock; failover has taken up to 30 seconds in drills.
- Topic shipment-status.v2: 24 partitions, keyed by shipment_id, replication factor 3, producer acks=all.
- Consumers: each consumer records processed event_id values in a dedupe table (processed_events) inside the same transaction as its own side effects. Entries are kept for 7 days.
- Dead-letter topic shipment-status.dlq: a message goes there after 5 failed attempts with exponential backoff starting at 2 seconds.

4. Delivery guarantees
Dockhand is at-least-once, not exactly-once. The relay can publish a batch and crash before it sets published_at; on restart that batch is published again. Duplicates are expected and are removed by the consumer-side dedupe on event_id. Ordering is guaranteed per shipment only (same key, same partition). There is no ordering across shipments.

5. Service levels
Target: p99 time from outbox commit to consumer receipt under 4 seconds. Measured in October 2024: p50 0.6 s, p99 2.9 s, excluding relay failovers.

6. Alternatives considered
- Debezium change data capture: rejected for v1 because the platform team did not run Kafka Connect yet, and we did not want to own a Connect cluster for one pipeline. Revisit in 2025.
- Publishing directly from the request with retries: rejected; it cannot close the gap between commit and publish.
- SQS FIFO: rejected because the billing and settlement teams already consumed from Kafka, and FIFO throughput limits per message group would have needed careful sharding.

7. Known limitations
- The single active relay is a throughput ceiling; load tests showed it saturates near 3,000 events per second.
- JSON payloads carry a schema_version field, but there is no schema registry; breaking changes are coordinated by hand.
- The dedupe window is 7 days, so replaying older messages from the DLQ requires a manual override flag.

8. Open questions
- Whether to move the relay to logical replication once Kafka Connect exists.
- Whether 24 partitions is enough if the Tern consumers need more parallelism.

items.question: Okay, you've had the escrow holds problem for a few minutes. Before you write any code, tell me how you'd get the max number of overlapping holds and the first time it happens.
items.answer: Sweep line over the endpoints. I turn each hold into two events: a start at `start` with +1, and an end at `end` with -1. Sort the events by time, and at the same time process all the -1s before the +1s, so a hold ending at 40 and one starting at 40 don't count as overlapping. Then I walk the sorted events keeping a running count, track the max, and record the first time that max is hit. That's O(n log n) time for the sort and O(n) space for the events.

items.question: Quick one. for i := 1; i < n; i *= 2 { for j := 0; j < i; j++ { sum++ } }. That's n log n, right?
items.answer: Not quite. The outer loop runs log n times, but the inner loop isn't n each time, it's i, and i doubles: 1, 2, 4, 8, up to n. So the total work is 1 + 2 + 4 + ... + n, which is about 2n. That's **O(n)**, not n log n. The n log n case is when the inner loop runs a full n for each of the log n outer iterations.

items.question: You partitioned that big events table by month. How did you keep event IDs unique across the partitions, and what happened to queries that didn't filter on time?
items.answer: The load_events table was partitioned by month in PostgreSQL, and the event ID stayed the primary key on the parent table, so uniqueness was enforced across all partitions rather than per partition. Queries that didn't filter on time couldn't prune, so they scanned every partition, which is the tradeoff I accepted since the nightly vacuum dropped from 4 hours to 35 minutes.

items.role: USER: the candidate. OTHER PARTY: the technical interviewer. Natively: explanation, reasoning, code, complexity, system design the candidate can use. Résumé/JD (if in evidence) are the candidate's own.
items.question: Tell me about a real production incident from when you were on call. What broke, how did you figure it out, and what did you change afterward?
items.answer: I was on a six-person on-call rotation at Larkspur Freight, and the incident I learned the most from was around the load_events table. Nightly vacuum had crept up to four hours, and it was starting to collide with our settlement jobs. I dug into the table and found it had grown to 1.9 billion rows with no partitioning, so I partitioned it by month. Vacuum dropped from four hours to 35 minutes. Afterward I wrote up the runbook for it, part of the first set of 14 our team had.

items.role: USER: the candidate. OTHER PARTY: the technical interviewer. Natively: explanation, reasoning, code, complexity, system design the candidate can use. Résumé/JD (if in evidence) are the candidate's own.
items.question: Here's the problem. You get an array of integers, which can be negative, and a target k. Return the length of the longest contiguous subarray that sums to exactly k. Start with brute force, then give me the optimal approach, then the time and space, and then tell me whether a sliding window would work here and why or why not.
items.answer:
Brute force is to fix each starting index i, then extend j from i to the end, keeping a running sum and checking whether it equals k at each step. That's correct because every contiguous subarray is exactly some pair (i, j), so checking all of them can't miss the answer. It runs in O(n²) time and O(1) extra space, and it's slow because for each of the n starts we re-walk the rest of the array, redoing sums we've already computed.

The optimal approach is a prefix-sum hash map. Let prefix[i] be the sum of the first i elements. A subarray from i to j sums to k exactly when prefix[j+1] minus prefix[i] equals k, so for each position we want to know whether prefix[j+1] minus k has been seen before. I walk the array once, keeping a running sum, and store in a hash map the earliest index at which each prefix sum appeared. At each step I check whether runningSum minus k is in the map, and if it is, the candidate length is the current index minus that stored index. I only store a prefix sum the first time I see it, since the earliest occurrence gives the longest subarray. That's O(n) time and O(n) space for the map.

A sliding window does not work here, and the reason is the negatives. The window technique relies on the sum being monotonic as you move the right pointer: grow while the sum is under k, shrink while it's over. With negative numbers, adding an element can decrease the sum and removing one can increase it, so the two-pointer invariant breaks and you can't decide when to move the left edge. If the array were all non-negative, sliding window would work in O(n) time and O(1) space.

items.role: USER: the candidate. OTHER PARTY: the technical interviewer. Natively: explanation, reasoning, code, complexity, system design the candidate can use. Résumé/JD (if in evidence) are the candidate's own.
items.question: So, Dockhand. The outbox means you never publish the same event twice, right? Walk me through how the relay guarantees that.
items.answer: No, it's at-least-once, not exactly-once. The relay polls unpublished rows every 250 ms in batches of up to 500, ordered by created_at, publishes them, then sets published_at. If it crashes after publishing but before setting published_at, that batch gets published again on restart. So duplicates are expected, and they're removed on the consumer side by dedupe on event_id, recorded in the processed_events table in the same transaction as the consumer's own side effects. The dedupe window is 7 days, so replaying anything older from the DLQ needs a manual override flag.

items.role: USER: the candidate. OTHER PARTY: the technical interviewer. Natively: explanation, reasoning, code, complexity, system design the candidate can use. Résumé/JD (if in evidence) are the candidate's own.
items.question: Design the nightly settlement batch for a marketplace like ours. It takes the day of ledger entries, computes payouts per grower, sends them to the bank, and has to be done before banks open. How do you split up the work, how do you make a rerun safe if it dies halfway, and what do you page on?
items.answer:
I'd split it into three phases with a durable workflow driving them, since you already run Temporal. Phase one is a read-only aggregation pass: for each grower, pull the day's ledger entries and compute the payout, writing results into a settlement run table keyed by run date and grower. Phase two is the bank submission, one idempotent call per grower with a stable idempotency key derived from run date plus grower, so a retry never double-pays. Phase three is reconciliation, matching bank acknowledgements back to the run and flagging anything unmatched for Finance.

For rerun safety, the whole thing is idempotent and resumable. Each grower's row moves through explicit states, pending, computed, submitted, confirmed, failed, and the batch only advances rows that aren't already confirmed. If it dies halfway, you restart the run for that date and it picks up where it left off, skipping confirmed growers and retrying the rest. The bank call carries the idempotency key so even a submission that succeeded but wasn't recorded won't pay twice. I'd also make the run itself a single row with a status and a lock, so two schedulers can't start the same date concurrently.

On paging: the batch not finishing before banks open is the top alert, that's a hard deadline. Then a spike in failed or unconfirmed submissions, and any reconciliation mismatch where the ledger total doesn't equal the sum of payouts. I'd page on those three, and just ticket on individual grower failures that retry cleanly.

items.role: USER: the candidate. OTHER PARTY: the technical interviewer. Natively: explanation, reasoning, code, complexity, system design the candidate can use. Résumé/JD (if in evidence) are the candidate's own.
items.question: This is supposed to return the first index where a[i] >= target, but it hangs on some inputs. lo, hi := 0, len(a)-1; for lo < hi { mid := (lo + hi) / 2; if a[mid] < target { lo = mid } else { hi = mid - 1 } }; return lo. What's wrong with it?
items.answer: Two bugs. When `a[mid] < target` you set `lo = mid`, so if `hi == lo + 1` and `a[lo] < target`, mid stays lo and it loops forever. And `hi = mid - 1` skips the answer, since mid itself could be the first index. Use `lo = mid + 1` and `hi = mid`, and return `lo` after the loop.

items.question: Why not Debezium?
conversation: INTERVIEWER (heard): So, Dockhand. The outbox means you never publish the same event twice, right? Walk me through how the relay guarantees that.

NATIVELY: No, it's at-least-once, not exactly-once. The relay polls unpublished rows every 250 ms in batches of up to 500, ordered by created_at, publishes them, then sets published_at. If it crashes after publishing but before setting published_at, that batch gets published again on restart. So duplicates are expected, and they're removed on the consumer side by dedupe on event_id, recorded in the processed_events table in the same transaction as the consumer's own side effects. The dedupe window is 7 days, so replaying anything older from the DLQ needs a manual override flag.
items.answer: We did look at it. Debezium reads the WAL, so it's cleaner in that it doesn't poll, but it ties the pipeline to PostgreSQL's replication slot and its own connector lifecycle, and we wanted the publish path to stay in our code where we control ordering, batching and the DLQ. The outbox also keeps the event and the business row in one transaction, which is the property we actually needed.

items.role: USER: the candidate. OTHER PARTY: the technical interviewer. Natively: explanation, reasoning, code, complexity, system design the candidate can use. Résumé/JD (if in evidence) are the candidate's own.
items.question: Tell me about Dockhand. Roughly how many events a day was it handling, and why did you go with Kafka for it?
items.answer:
Dockhand is a Kafka event pipeline I designed at Larkspur Freight. It processes about 2.3 million shipment status events a day, and I used a transactional outbox table so we don't get duplicate writes.

On why Kafka: the honest answer is the evidence I have doesn't spell out the reasoning, so I'd frame it as what I was weighing. Shipment status is a high-volume stream of events, and Kafka gives you durable, ordered, replayable logs with consumer groups, so multiple downstream services can read the same events independently. The outbox pattern pairs with that to keep writes exactly-once-ish.

items.role: USER: the candidate. OTHER PARTY: the technical interviewer. Natively: explanation, reasoning, code, complexity, system design the candidate can use. Résumé/JD (if in evidence) are the candidate's own.
items.question: he wants a double entry ledger schema in postgres. core tables plus the constraints that keep it balanced
items.answer:
Two core tables: **accounts** with an id, name, and type, and **entries** with account_id, a transaction_id, and an amount. Store debits positive and credits negative, or keep a direction column.

The balance constraint is the key one: sum of amounts grouped by transaction_id must equal zero, enforced with a deferred constraint trigger so it checks at commit, not per row.

items.role: USER: the candidate. OTHER PARTY: the technical interviewer. Natively: explanation, reasoning, code, complexity, system design the candidate can use. Résumé/JD (if in evidence) are the candidate's own.
items.question: Now say holds come in one at a time off a stream and some get cancelled early. How do you keep that answer current without redoing the whole sweep?
conversation: INTERVIEWER (heard): Okay, you've had the escrow holds problem for a few minutes. Before you write any code, tell me how you'd get the max number of overlapping holds and the first time it happens.

NATIVELY: Sweep line over the endpoints. I turn each hold into two events: a start at `start` with +1, and an end at `end` with -1. Sort the events by time, and at the same time process all the -1s before the +1s, so a hold ending at 40 and one starting at 40 don't count as overlapping. Then I walk the sorted events keeping a running count, track the max, and record the first time that max is hit. That's O(n log n) time for the sort and O(n) space for the events.
INTERVIEWER (heard): Run that on example one out loud. What do you get?

NATIVELY: I don't have example one in front of me, so I can't run the numbers on it. If you give me the holds, I'll walk the sweep: sort the events, process ends before starts at the same minute, and track the running count and the first minute it peaks.
items.answer: For a stream, I'd keep the sweep's state incrementally instead of rebuilding it. Maintain a balanced BST or a Fenwick tree over the compressed time coordinates, keyed by minute, holding the running count of active holds. An insert adds +1 at its start and -1 at its end, a cancel removes those two events. Each update is O(log n), and I keep the max and its earliest minute in the tree so the answer stays current after every event.

items.role: USER: the candidate. OTHER PARTY: the technical interviewer. Natively: explanation, reasoning, code, complexity, system design the candidate can use. Résumé/JD (if in evidence) are the candidate's own.
items.question: Postgres runs at serializable by default, right? So which anomalies can you still hit?
items.answer: Actually, Postgres defaults to **read committed**, not serializable. Serializable is opt-in per transaction, and even then it's SSI, so it prevents write skew and lost updates but you can still hit serialization failures that force a retry, plus anomalies outside the database like non-repeatable reads across separate connections or stale reads from replicas.

items.question: What about space?
conversation: INTERVIEWER: Okay, so you wrote Fibonacci top-down, plain recursion with a hash map as the memo.
USER (spoken): Right, and each value from zero to n gets computed once, so time is linear.
INTERVIEWER: Yep, I agree on time.
items.answer: Space is **O(n)** for the memo table, since we store one entry per value from zero to n. The recursion stack adds another **O(n)** in the worst case, so total space is O(n).

items.question: Run that on example one out loud. What do you get?
conversation: INTERVIEWER (heard): Okay, you've had the escrow holds problem for a few minutes. Before you write any code, tell me how you'd get the max number of overlapping holds and the first time it happens.

NATIVELY: Sweep line over the endpoints. I turn each hold into two events: a start at `start` with +1, and an end at `end` with -1. Sort the events by time, and at the same time process all the -1s before the +1s, so a hold ending at 40 and one starting at 40 don't count as overlapping. Then I walk the sorted events keeping a running count, track the max, and record the first time that max is hit. That's O(n log n) time for the sort and O(n) space for the events.
items.answer: I don't have example one in front of me, so I can't run the numbers on it. If you give me the holds, I'll walk the sweep: sort the events, process ends before starts at the same minute, and track the running count and the first minute it peaks.
